newsitem.title: USA: EPA's Browner targets big polluters on new air rule.
newsitem.headline: EPA's Browner targets big polluters on new air rule.

text.p: The top U.S. environmental official Thursday sought to reassure small businesses and farmers that they would not be hammered with new costs as states move to meet new smog and soot standards set this week.

The Environmental Protection Agency on Wednesday signed a rule setting strict new limits on smog-forming ozone and fine particles. Counties and cities will have to start meeting the new smog standard in 2004 and the soot standard in 2005, with enforcement beginning a few years later.

"What we believe ... is that focusing on the largest sources, the combustion sources, the large utilities, you can get the kind of pollution reductions you need, and you can do it in the most cost-effective manner," said EPA Administrator Carol Browner.

Speaking at a Centre for National Policy breakfast, where labour, agriculture, and small business representatives raised concern about the economic costs of the tough new standards, Browner said imposing pollution controls on farms and small companies would not be the cheapest way to meet the standards.

"We're not going to do anything like that, I can assure you, and I would be surprised if you could find a governor or mayor who would do anything like that," she said. "It's just not going to happen."
Industry groups have complained that Browner has made those promises to other sectors, when in fact it will be up to states to decide how they plan to comply with the contrversial new air rules.

Utilities and manufacturers have estimated they will have to spend billions of dollars to curb smog-forming emissions, but Browner said cost predictions of meeting clean air standards in the past had all turned out to be too high.

She pointed to sulphur dioxide emissions cuts, which utilities had expected to cost $1,000 per ton and EPA had pegged at $600 per ton, but have actually cost less than $100 per ton, with the help of an emissions credit trading scheme, technology improvements and low-sulphur coal supplies.

The Clinton administration believes the average cost of reducing each ton of smog-forming emissions will be $2,500. Backing those claims, the administration set a $10,000 cap on the cost per ton of cutting emissions, EPA officials said.

If a plant that is required to reduce pollution can prove that it cannot find a way to do it for less than $10,000 per ton of emissions, either through trading pollution credits or using new technology, then it would have to contribute $10,000 per ton of targeted emissions to a fund.

State or local governments would then use that money to buy cleaner technologies, such as alternative fuel vehicles for government fleets or more energy-efficient technologies for government buildings, to help reduce pollution.
"We're not convinced anyone will have to pay into (the fund)," EPA Assistant Administrator Fred Hansen told Reuters after Browner spoke.

According to a two-year study done by 37 Eastern states, curbing pollution from power plants would cost $600 to $3,500 per ton of emissions, while cutting smog-forming emissions from cars and trucks would cost at least $15,000 per ton.
